ATTORNEY-CLIENT PRIVILEGED - PREPARED AT THE DIRECTION OF THE AUDIT COMMITTEE
MEMORANDUM
To: Audit Committee (L. Fong, R. Castellano, D. Okwu). From: Office of the Chief Legal Officer. Date: April __, 2025. Re: Apex acquisition fiduciary analysis.

1. SHORT ANSWER
If the Board approved the deal on the current track, Delaware courts would very likely not view the process as adequate. There is no disinterested-director approval, no empowered committee, no committee-level advisors, the interested director chaired the discussion, and the only valuation is a preliminary, management-retained, success-fee analysis. But nothing has been approved or signed, so these defects are curable if the Committee acts before any binding step (exclusivity in the draft term sheet binds on signature). Caveats: this rests on ten matter documents; my office is management's counsel and should not be the Committee's adviser; see Part 10 on verification limits.

2. KEY FACTS
Dr. Whitfield, director since 2015 and Chairman since 2018, is sole trustee of the Whitfield Family Trust (beneficiaries: his three children), which owns 62% of Apex and would receive about $29.45M of the $47.5M ($34.0M cash, $8.5M stock, $5.0M all-or-nothing revenue earnout). He also owns about 5.4% of VHS. Other benefits: release of his $6.2M guarantee (VHS indemnifies him if not released); a three-year employment agreement ($375,000 plus up to $150,000 bonus) for his brother-in-law Granville (23% seller); and the Trust serves as Sellers' Representative. On April 4 he distributed his own Transaction Overview, presented, presided throughout and answered questions for about 30 minutes; no recusal was offered; no vote. His memo promises recusal only from "any final Board vote."

3. STANDARD OF REVIEW
(a) Controller status. The record does not show Whitfield is a controlling stockholder: 5.4% of VHS voting stock and a long chairmanship. Amended DGCL 144 defines a controller as a holder of majority voting power, or power to elect a board majority, or at least one-third voting power plus managerial authority equivalent to majority control. Tesla (Del. 2023) shows control is fact-specific (a 22% holder was a conceivable controller), so confirm voting power and board ties. I treat this as an interested-director transaction and reserve the controller question.
(b) Common law. A director on both sides triggers entire fairness (fair dealing and fair price, examined as a whole): Weinberger v. UOP, 457 A.2d 701 (Del. 1983); Cinerama v. Technicolor, 663 A.2d 1156 (Del. 1995). Defendants bear the burden unless cleansed.
(c) SB 21 (signed March 25, 2025). New 144(a) protects an interested director transaction fully disclosed and approved in good faith and without gross negligence by (i) a majority of disinterested directors where the board has a disinterested majority, (ii) a committee of at least two disinterested directors, or (iii) an informed, uncoerced majority of votes cast by disinterested stockholders; or if the transaction is fair. Directors the board determined independent under Nasdaq rules are presumed disinterested, rebuttable only by substantial and particularized facts (144(d)(2)). If Whitfield were a controller, 144(b) requires committee approval or a disinterested-stockholder vote, whereas pre-amendment MFW (Kahn v. M&F Worldwide, 88 A.3d 635 (Del. 2014); extended by In re Match Group (Del. 2024)) required both. The amendments reach pre-enactment acts absent pending litigation; the Delaware Supreme Court upheld them in Rutledge v. Clearway (Feb. 27, 2026). Chancery has withheld the safe harbor at the pleading stage where the board process was plausibly grossly negligent (Dodiya v. Franklin, Aug. 2026), so the process must be real.
(d) Charter. Article VIII exculpates directors only for care claims; loyalty, bad faith and improper personal benefit are carved out, and nothing exculpates officers (relevant to CEO Park). Article IX gives no cover: the corporate-opportunity waiver excludes the procurement and distribution of medical devices. Apex (formed 2017, while Whitfield was a director) operates in that field, a loyalty issue to investigate.
(e) Bylaws Article XII. Whitfield is a Related Person; the deal exceeds $5M, so 12.3 (Audit Committee approval) and 12.5 (majority of disinterested directors) both apply. Article XII supplements, and 12.6 preserves, fiduciary claims. The Audit Committee's bylaw role is review and approval with no express power to negotiate, reject or retain advisors, so it is not a special committee. Granville is not an "Immediate Family Member" (brother-in-law is outside spouse/parent/child/sibling), so his employment is reviewed through Whitfield's interest under 12.3(c)(iv), not as a separate trigger.

4. PROCESS DEFICIENCIES
1. Fair dealing: Yes, Whitfield's April 4 role is a significant fair-dealing deficiency (initiation, structure, information flow, deliberation), aggravated by his statement that Ridgeline "confirms the fairness" when Ridgeline disclaims any fairness opinion. His disclosure of his interest, the Granville tie and the guarantee mitigates. It is curable because no approval occurred.
2. No committee or mandate; management drafted the term sheet, to be signed by Park, who reports to a board chaired by Whitfield.
3. Advisors: Whitfield recommended Hargrove & Pemberton, VHS's regular counsel; the CLO's office is management counsel. Neither is independent counsel for a committee.
4. Omissions: neither the Overview nor the minutes mention the existing MSA, its pricing, or its approval gap; no alternatives or market check.
5. Term sheet: Whitfield controls post-closing disputes as Sellers' Representative; several-only indemnity capped at 15%, 10% escrow; earnout is revenue-only, administered under Granville (brother-in-law) with intercompany revenue (VHS purchases) unresolved, enabling manipulation; closing condition requires only "Board (or committee)" approval, not Article XII; binding exclusivity; June 15 target creates time pressure.
6. Valuation advisor retained by management (Part 5).
7. Rivera said he "saw no issues" and urged speed, with no critical engagement.

5. RIDGELINE RELIABILITY
Independence: engaged by the CFO for "senior management"; $350,000 advisory fee plus $1.2M contingent on closing (about 77% of fees); three prior VHS deals; reliance on Apex-supplied data without verification; no duty to update; use limited to management. Advisor conflicts undermine an informed process (RBC Capital v. Jervis, 129 A.3d 816 (Del. 2015); In re Del Monte, 25 A.3d 813 (Del. Ch. 2011)). It is preliminary, not a fairness opinion.
Substance: (i) $2.8M of unverified adjustments lift EBITDA 46% ($6.1M to $8.9M). The $1.2M "above-market lease" add-back depends on the lessor (Lone Star Properties LP, relationship to Whitfield unknown); without it the multiple is about 6.17x, above Ridgeline's 5.8x ceiling. (ii) Apex's EBITDA includes VHS's roughly $470,000 overpayment (IA estimate), worth about $2.5M at 5.34x, and which disappears on consolidation. (iii) The $0.3M excess-CEO-pay add-back conflicts with Granville's proposed $375,000-plus-bonus package. (iv) Ridgeline's stated DCF inputs (FCF $5.8M-$7.9M, 11.5% WACC, 2.5% growth) compute to roughly $77M, not the reported $46.3M (my calculation), so the DCF is unexplained. (v) It compares enterprise value to the equity price without addressing Apex's about $4.1M revolver debt. (vi) Records inconsistencies to authenticate: Ridgeline's address and phone differ between letter and memo; the CFO is "Hartwell" in the letter but "Holloway" in the minutes (Holloway also signs as Director of Internal Audit).
Conclusion: not a basis for a fully informed approval. The Committee needs its own advisor.

6. EXISTING GOVERNANCE ISSUES: THE APEX MSA
Internal Audit (Report IA-2025-007, preliminary: 25 SKUs, about 60% of spend) found the 2019 MSA was approved by Procurement alone, never reached the Related-Party Register, the Audit Committee or the Board, and was renewed annually; FY2024 purchases were $4.7M (cumulative estimated above $20M), priced 8-12% above market. This violated 12.3(a), which also bars continuation without approval, so the Committee should act now. Under 12.6 the MSA is not void but must be reviewed and ratified, modified or terminated promptly. On a series-of-transactions reading, 12.5 Board approval was also required. Significance: possible loyalty claims against Whitfield for overpayment (limitations and tolling need analysis), negotiating leverage, and a price input (overstated EBITDA; weak "synergy" thesis, since Apex is 3.8% of VHS supply spend). Keep MSA remediation separate from the acquisition; release no claims in the deal.
Disclosure: the April 1 proxy calls the MSA "arm's length" and "competitive" with no benchmarking, and states there are no currently proposed related-party transactions, although the Apex acquisition was under way since February 20 and Ridgeline engaged March 3. That raises Regulation S-K Item 404 and Rule 14a-9 questions; securities counsel should assess corrective disclosure promptly. Because the CLO's office requested the March 25 audit before the filing, outside counsel should review that history. Accurate disclosure is also a precondition to any 144 safe harbor.

7. RIVERA AND THE DIRECTOR POOL
Independence asks whether a director is beholden to or too close to the interested party. Delaware County v. Sanchez, 124 A.3d 1017 (Del. 2015), and Marchand v. Barnhill, 212 A.3d 805 (Del. 2019) (about $450,000 of family charitable giving) show gifts and ties can raise pleading-stage doubt; Sandys v. Pincus, 152 A.3d 124 (Del. 2016), shows not every tie suffices. About $2M over five years to a nonprofit where Rivera sits on the advisory board, plus his posture on April 4, creates real vulnerability, though the 144(d)(2) presumption helps if the Board determined him independent. Unknown: his compensation, Whitfield's share of foundation funding, personal ties. Recommendation: exclude him from the committee; do not rely on his vote for any disinterested majority. Defensible pool, subject to refreshed questionnaires: Fong, Okwu, Castellano (independent per proxy), Chen and Pittman (independent per minutes). Cross's status is unstated; Park is management. Excluding Whitfield, Park, Cross and Rivera leaves five of nine, a thin disinterested majority.

8. RECOMMENDED STEPS, IN SEQUENCE
1. Immediately: do not sign the term sheet or exclusivity; halt management price discussions; litigation hold; limit circulation.
2. Whitfield steps back from all deliberation, chair duties and information flow on Apex (independent presiding director); he acts only as counterparty, and management takes direction from the committee.
3. Disinterested directors adopt a Board resolution forming a Special Committee of three vetted directors, with exclusive authority to evaluate, negotiate, reject, consider alternatives and retain advisors, and a Board commitment not to approve without its recommendation, before substantive negotiation.
4. The Committee retains independent counsel (no Whitfield or VHS history; vet Hargrove & Pemberton if considered) and an independent financial advisor on a fixed, non-contingent fee, delivering a written fairness opinion to the Committee. Ridgeline may supply data but cannot be relied upon.
5. Audit Committee completes the comprehensive MSA review and ratifies, reprices or terminates under 12.3 and 12.6; investigate Lone Star lease, Granville compensation and Apex's formation history.
6. Securities counsel evaluates corrective disclosure.
7. Renegotiate: independent Sellers' Representative; earnout excluding intercompany revenue; joint and several or better-secured indemnity; no VHS indemnity for the guarantee; Compensation Committee review of Granville terms; price adjusted for MSA overpricing and EBITDA diligence; closing conditions requiring Committee approval, Article XII approvals and the fairness opinion.
8. Approval: Committee recommendation, then Article XII 12.3 and 12.5 approvals by disinterested directors, with Whitfield absent. A majority-of-disinterested-stockholders vote is not required for a non-controller under 144(a) but is a worthwhile second layer if controller status or disclosure issues remain unresolved.
9. Move the June 15 target as needed; the Committee should not be rushed.

9. LITIGATION RISK
Current process: high. No safe harbor is available, entire fairness would apply with the burden on defendants, and the April 4 minutes, the Ridgeline terms and the MSA findings would be plaintiff exhibits (post-SB 21 books-and-records access still includes minutes and board materials). Whitfield faces unexculpated loyalty exposure; independent directors face bad-faith theories if they rubber-stamp; Ridgeline and Apex face aiding-and-abetting risk. Remediated process: low to moderate. A properly formed, informed committee with independent advisors and a real ability to say no should secure 144(a) protection or at least shift the fairness inquiry decisively; residual risk: disclosure accuracy, gross negligence allegations, controller arguments, MSA claims.

10. UNRESOLVED / LIMITS
Official DGCL 144 text was not retrieved (site blocked); subsection references come from secondary summaries and should be confirmed. Cases are cited from search summaries, not full opinions. Open facts: Whitfield's voting power and board influence; Cross's independence; Rivera's foundation role; lessor identity; DCF discrepancy; Nasdaq independence determinations; annual meeting date. Item 404 is cited from general knowledge, not verified here.

claims.text: Absent cleansing, a transaction with Whitfield on both sides faces entire fairness; current process has no disinterested approval and would likely not withstand scrutiny.

The record does not show Whitfield is a controller (5.4%); treat as interested-director transaction but verify and reserve; SB 21 safe harbors (committee of 2+ disinterested directors, majority disinterested directors, or stockholder vote) are available if process is genuine.
Whitfield's April 4 chairing is a significant fair-dealing deficiency, curable because nothing was approved; he should be recused from deliberation and chair duties.

Ridgeline is not a reliable basis: management-retained, contingent fee, unverified adjustments, lease add-back dependency (6.17x without it), VHS overpayment in EBITDA, DCF inconsistency, EV/equity mismatch.
The MSA violated Bylaws Art. XII for five-plus years; Committee must review and ratify, modify or terminate; bears on price and leverage.
The April 1 proxy characterization of the MSA and its statement of no proposed related-party transactions raise disclosure issues requiring securities counsel review.
Rivera should be excluded from the committee; defensible pool is Fong, Okwu, Castellano, Chen, Pittman subject to vetting.

Form a fully empowered special committee, retain independent counsel and fixed-fee financial advisor, remediate MSA, renegotiate terms, obtain Art. XII approvals; stockholder vote optional second layer.
Litigation risk is high under the current process and low to moderate if remediated.
Charter exculpation does not cover loyalty; Art. IX gives no waiver; Granville is outside the bylaw family definition but reviewed via Whitfield's interest.
Source documents contain inconsistencies (Ridgeline address, CFO name) and legal citations are from search summaries pending official-text verification.
